item.title: Anthropic Said to Choose Nasdaq for Much-Anticipated IPO Listing
item.author: Bailey Lipschultz
item.description:
Anthropic Said to Choose Nasdaq for Much-Anticipated IPO Listing
2026-09-14
Por Bailey Lipschultz
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/anthropic-said-choose-nasdaq-much-180359465.html
(Bloomberg) -- Anthropic PBC has picked Nasdaq as its listing venue ahead of a potential record-setting initial public offering, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The Claude chatbot maker is seeking to raise as much as or more than SpaceX in an IPO that could take place as soon as October, people familiar with the preparations have said.
A Nasdaq listing would mark another win for the company this year with four of the largest US IPOs taking place on the exchange, including SpaceX's record-setting $86.3 billion offering in June. SK Hynix Inc. followed a few weeks later after it raised $26.5 billion in an July debut.
Business Insider reported earlier on Anthropic's choice of Nasdaq. Anthropic didn't immediately respond to a request for comment and Nasdaq declined to comment.
Anthropic's IPO preparations came as OpenAI Inc. CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Elon Musk on Saturday all voiced the need to slow the pace of AI development due to escalating risks from the technology. Altman told Fortune in an interview that his company won't go public this year, citing safety concerns.
Anthropic was set to finalize a $15 billion revolving credit facility earlier this month, Bloomberg News reported.
The AI race has fired up the IPO market, with US listings this year raising $160.6 billion, excluding blank-check firms and other financial vehicles, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That's the most raised in a year since 2021, the data show.
Anthropic is on track to generate annualized revenue of over $65 billion based on its current performance, up more than sevenfold from its pace at the end of last year, Bloomberg News reported.
--With assistance from Katherine Doherty and Shirin Ghaffary.
Most Read from Bloomberg Businessweek
2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: Atentados del 11-S: "El problema con esta foto es que tenemos ganas de decir que es hermosa"
item.author: Por RFI
item.description:
Atentados del 11-S: "El problema con esta foto es que tenemos ganas de decir que es hermosa"
2026-09-12
Por Por RFI
https://www.rfi.fr/es/cultura/20260911-atentados-del-11-s-el-problema-con-esta-foto-es-que-tenemos-ganas-de-decir-que-es-hermosa
Atentados del 11-S: "El problema con esta foto es que tenemos ganas de decir que es hermosa"
El 11 de septiembre de 2001, un periodista de la Associated Press fue enviado al pie de las Torres Gemelas. El resultado fue una de las fotos más famosas del fotoperiodismo. Sin embargo, la imagen fue censurada casi de inmediato, considerada demasiado impactante por la opinión pública estadounidense. En su libro L'homme qui tombe (el hombre que cae), el periodista Philippe Lecaplain repasa la historia de esta fotografía.
Primera modificación: Última modificación:
Por Jean-Baptiste Breen
Hace 25 años, cuando el vuelo 175 de United Airlines acababa de abrir la Torre Sur del World Trade Center, Richard Drew salió del metro de Nueva York. El fotógrafo de la agencia de noticias estadounidense Associated Press corrió hacia los edificios de donde se elevaba una densa columna de humo negro.
Cuando se acercó lo máximo posible a las Torres Gemelas devoradas por las llamas, el hombre de 50 años se refugió tras el objetivo de su cámara. El periodista se centró en los "saltadores" (jumpers) que se lanzaban hacia la muerte desde las ventanas de las torres, huyendo de los vapores asfixiantes del fuego.
Entre las tomas de Richard Drew destaca la de un hombre en caída libre, con la espalda recta y las piernas ligeramente dobladas, como si estuviera suspendido en pleno vuelo. Esta imagen, sin duda una de las más famosas de la tragedia, fue sin embargo objeto de una censura casi total, que sigue vigente en gran medida hoy en día.
En su libro L'homme qui tombe (el hombre que cae), publicado el pasado junio por Librisphaera y seleccionado para el premio Roman News, Philippe Lecaplain, periodista de RFI, repasa la historia de esta fotografía, un símbolo oculto del trauma del 11 de septiembre de 2001.
"Podemos identificarnos"
Aparte de la historia del fotógrafo Richard Drew, Lecaplain repasa la investigación llevada a cabo por varios periodistas para identificar al hombre desconocido inmortalizado en medio de su caída en la fotografía, aunque, a pesar de varias pistas prometedoras, hasta ahora no se ha llegado a una conclusión definitiva. Un misterio que aún alimenta el aspecto perturbador de esta fotografía.
A nivel puramente técnico, "la foto es perfecta", comenta Philippe Lecaplain. A cada lado, las torres norte y sur forman un fondo simétrico salpicado por líneas paralelas, divididas en su centro por la silueta del hombre que cae. "Hoy diríamos '¡pero, es IA!'", exclama el autor.
"Esta foto no muestra un cadáver. Un cadáver futuro, sin duda, pero no un cadáver", enfatiza. "El hombre sigue vivo y parece sano, elegante, casi apuesto". Así que, casi por reflejo, "podemos identificarnos", continúa Lecaplain. "Ante esta foto, me pregunto: ¿qué habría hecho yo en lugar de la gente en las torres ese día?", recalca.
Esta misma cuestión, tan morbosa como inevitable, es sin duda el origen de la censura sistemática impuesta a esta fotografía inmediatamente después de su publicación. Al menos esta es la tesis de Philippe Lecaplain. No solo devuelve a los estadounidenses al horror de los ataques, sino que también les ofrece la posibilidad de imaginarse en el lugar de este "saltador".
Un reflejo insoportable
En los días posteriores al 11-S, los periódicos que habían decidido publicar la fotografía de Richard Drew se vieron abrumados por cartas mordaces de lectores decepcionados, tristes o enfadados. Por lo tanto, desapareció casi de inmediato de la circulación, mientras que algunos títulos de prensa llegaron a publicar cartas de disculpa en un intento de apaciguar el descontento. "Su audaz y valiente sesgo periodístico termina donde comienza el inconmensurable duelo nacional", comenta Lecaplain.
¿Qué podría s
[Transcripcion recortada]

https://www.rfi.fr/es/cultura/20260911-atentados-del-11-s-el-problema-con-esta-foto-es-que-tenemos-ganas-de-decir-que-es-hermosa
Atentados del 11-S: "El problema con esta foto es que tenemos ganas de decir que es hermosa"
El 11 de septiembre de 2001, un periodista de la Associated Press fue enviado al pie de las Torres Gemelas. El resultado fue una de las fotos más famosas del fotoperiodismo. Sin embargo, la imagen fue censurada casi de inmediato, considerada demasiado impactante por la opinión pública estadounidense. En su libro L'homme qui tombe (el hombre que cae), el periodista Philippe Lecaplain repasa la historia de esta fotografía.
Primera modificación: Última modificación:
Por Jean-Baptiste Breen
Hace 25 años, cuando el vuelo 175 de United Airlines acababa de abrir la Torre Sur del World Trade Center, Richard Drew salió del metro de Nueva York. El fotógrafo de la agencia de noticias estadounidense Associated Press corrió hacia los edificios de donde se elevaba una densa columna de humo negro.
Cuando se acercó lo máximo posible a las Torres Gemelas devoradas por las llamas, el hombre de 50 años se refugió tras el objetivo de su cámara. El periodista se centró en los "saltadores" (jumpers) que se lanzaban hacia la muerte desde las ventanas de las torres, huyendo de los vapores asfixiantes del fuego.
Entre las tomas de Richard Drew destaca la de un hombre en caída libre, con la espalda recta y las piernas ligeramente dobladas, como si estuviera suspendido en pleno vuelo. Esta imagen, sin duda una de las más famosas de la tragedia, fue sin embargo objeto de una censura casi total, que sigue vigente en gran medida hoy en día.
En su libro L'homme qui tombe (el hombre que cae), publicado el pasado junio por Librisphaera y seleccionado para el premio Roman News, Philippe Lecaplain, periodista de RFI, repasa la historia de esta fotografía, un símbolo oculto del trauma del 11 de septiembre de 2001.
"Podemos identificarnos"
Aparte de la historia del fotógrafo Richard Drew, Lecaplain repasa la investigación llevada a cabo por varios periodistas para identificar al hombre desconocido inmortalizado en medio de su caída en la fotografía, aunque, a pesar de varias pistas prometedoras, hasta ahora no se ha llegado a una conclusión definitiva. Un misterio que aún alimenta el aspecto perturbador de esta fotografía.
A nivel puramente técnico, "la foto es perfecta", comenta Philippe Lecaplain. A cada lado, las torres norte y sur forman un fondo simétrico salpicado por líneas paralelas, divididas en su centro por la silueta del hombre que cae. "Hoy diríamos '¡pero, es IA!'", exclama el autor.
"Esta foto no muestra un cadáver. Un cadáver futuro, sin duda, pero no un cadáver", enfatiza. "El hombre sigue vivo y parece sano, elegante, casi apuesto". Así que, casi por reflejo, "podemos identificarnos", continúa Lecaplain. "Ante esta foto, me pregunto: ¿qué habría hecho yo en lugar de la gente en las torres ese día?", recalca.
Esta misma cuestión, tan morbosa como inevitable, es sin duda el origen de la censura sistemática impuesta a esta fotografía inmediatamente después de su publicación. Al menos esta es la tesis de Philippe Lecaplain. No solo devuelve a los estadounidenses al horror de los ataques, sino que también les ofrece la posibilidad de imaginarse en el lugar de este "saltador".
Un reflejo insoportable
En los días posteriores al 11-S, los periódicos que habían decidido publicar la fotografía de Richard Drew se vieron abrumados por cartas mordaces de lectores decepcionados, tristes o enfadados. Por lo tanto, desapareció casi de inmediato de la circulación, mientras que algunos títulos de prensa llegaron a publicar cartas de disculpa en un intento de apaciguar el descontento. "Su audaz y valiente sesgo periodístico termina donde comienza el inconmensurable duelo nacional", comenta Lecaplain.

item.title: El opaco funcionamiento de Forbet, la casa de pronósticos deportivos con conexiones familiares a un equipo de fútbol en Ecuador
item.author: Evelyn Tapia
item.description:
El opaco funcionamiento de Forbet, la casa de pronósticos deportivos con conexiones familiares a un equipo de fútbol en Ecuador
2026-09-12
Por Evelyn Tapia
https://www.primicias.ec/deportes/apuestas-pronosticos-deportivos-forbet-control-superintendencia-companias-sociedad-civil-132202/
El opaco funcionamiento de Forbet, la casa de pronósticos deportivos con conexiones familiares a un equipo de fútbol en Ecuador
Forbet fue constituida en mayo de 2021. PRIMICIAS documentó que fue constituida como una sociedad civil, por lo que no reporta información de sus accionistas ni sus balances o situación financiera, y nadie la controla.
Imagen referencial de un jugador del Inter de Quito, con el uniforme que muestra a Forbet como auspiciante, 16 de agosto de 2026.
- Foto
Autor:
Redacción Primicias
Actualizada:
Compartir:
Forbet es una de las plataformas de pronósticos deportivos y casino virtual más conocidas en Ecuador, que auspicia, de hecho, a seis equipos de fútbol de la Serie A y de segunda categoría, uno de ellos es el Inter de Quito.
Pero ahora la casa de pronósticos está en el centro de la polémica, luego de que el exdueño del equipo Inter de Quito, Luis Chérrez, revelara a PRIMICIAS que la casa de pronósticos deportivos asumió el control del club, algo prohibido por la Ley del Deporte. La dirigencia de Inter de Quito, no obstante, asegura que Forbet es solo auspiciante.
"Ahora se hicieron cargo (del equipo Señor Montúfar) los de Forbet. Forbet es una casa de apuestas. Ellos manejan el equipo que se llama ahora Inter de Quito", dijo Chérrez.
Al igual que otros sitios de apuestas en línea, Forbet tiene una fuerte presencia en redes sociales, en donde promociona sus servicios con influencers nacionales e internacionales.
Pero es poco lo que se puede conocer sobre cómo opera esta empresa en Ecuador, cuántos ingresos tiene o quienes son sus representantes legales y accionistas actuales. Y esto se debe a que Forbet no está bajo en control de la Superintendencia de Compañías.
A diferencia de algunas de sus principales competidoras, Forbet decidió constituirse como una sociedad civil y no como una sociedad mercantil.
Las sociedades mercantiles (Compañías Limitadas, Sociedades Anónimas o por Acciones Simplificadas) están bajo el control de la Superintendencia de Compañías, explica el abogado societario Esteban Ortiz.
Y al estar bajo el control de la Superintendencia, las sociedades mercantiles están obligadas a presentar sus estados financieros anuales, balances, su nómina de accionistas y de administradores, así como auditorias e informes de la gerencia, añade Ortiz.
Según la Superintendencia de Compañías, hay 29 empresas con una actividad económica relacionada a pronósticos deportivos que están activas y bajo su control. De esas, 14 son Sociedades por Acciones Simplificadas (SAS), 13 son Sociedades Anónimas y dos son de Responsabilidad Limitada.
Sociedades en las que hay poca transparencia
En cambio, las sociedades civiles, como Forbet, no están obligadas a reportar su información ante la Superintendencia, que no las controla. Solo se constituyen con una escritura ante un notario y se inscriben en el Registro Mercantil, explica el abogado.
Para la abogada tributaria Yael Fierro, se trata de una figura que despierta inquietudes, "pues permite mantener en reserva esa información valiosa".
"Son sociedades en las que hay mucha opacidad y es muy común que, por esa poca transparencia, se use esta figura en empresas fantasmas que se dedican a la compra y venta de facturas"
Yael Fierro, abogada tributaria.
Este tipo de sociedades están definidas en el Código Civil, explica Ortiz y se pueden considerar, al igual que cualquier empresa, como una persona jurídica.
“Esto significa que tiene los mismos deberes que una Sociedad Anónima o una SAS, como afiliar a los empleados, tener RUC, pagar impuestos", añade el abogado.
Sin embargo, hay áreas grises en el Código Civil, por lo que hay poco control sobre estas sociedades,
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: Daniel Salcedo cambia de opinión y consiente en su extradición inmediata a Estados Unidos
item.author: Redacción Primicias
item.description:
Daniel Salcedo cambia de opinión y consiente en su extradición inmediata a Estados Unidos
2026-09-12
Por Redacción Primicias
https://www.primicias.ec/politica/daniel-salcedo-niega-extradicion-inmediata-estados-unidos-132206/
Daniel Salcedo cambia de opinión y consiente en su extradición inmediata a Estados Unidos
Durante su audiencia en la Corte Nacional de Justicia, en primera instancia, Daniel Salcedo no se acogió al procedimiento de extradición simplificada a Estados Unidos. Sin embargo, su abogado indicó que el sentenciado no había podido revisar el expediente de ese caso, y tras 10 minutos de receso, cambió su opinión y aceptó ser entregado.
Daniel Salcedo durante su audiencia de extradición a Estados Unidos, el 9 de septiembre de 2026.
- Foto
Captura de pantalla / CNJ
Autor:
Actualizada:
Compartir:
El sentenciado Daniel Salcedo Bonilla no aceptó de forma inmediata su extradición a Estados Unidos este 9 de septiembre de 2026. Durante la audiencia desarrollada a las 15:00 en la Sala Penal de la Corte Nacional de Justicia, en Quito, el recluso señaló que no se le ha permitido revisar los cargos del expediente estadounidense.
En primera instancia, Salcedo Bonilla negó su extradición inmediata a Estados Unidos. Por lo que Marco Rodríguez, presidente de la CNJ, dijo que el proceso se tramitará de manera ordinaria.
Sin embargo, Renato Montero, abogado de Salcedo, adujo la falta de conocimiento de los cinco cargos penales formulados en el Distrito Sur de Nueva York y solicitó tiempo para analizar la documentación.
El presidente Rodríguez negó suspender la diligencia para otra fecha, pero concedió un receso de 10 minutos para que Salcedo dialogue en privado con su abogado antes de volver a ser consultado.
Salcedo acumula seis condenas en Ecuador por peculado, lavado de activos, delincuencia organizada y fraude procesal. Además, permanece recluido e investigado como presunto implicado en el asesinato del excandidato presidencial Fernando Villavicencio.
Su negativa al trámite se produjo horas después de que RPHR, su excolaborador y testigo en el caso Villavicencio, consintiera su extradición en la misma alta corte.
Al rechazar el trámite simplificado, el expediente de Salcedo seguiría el procedimiento ordinario, por lo que la Presidencia de la Corte Nacional de Justicia debería evaluar y resolver sobre la procedencia de la solicitud del Gobierno norteamericano. Mientras que con el simplificado, el caso dependería de la Presidencia de la República.
La decisión final
Luego de ese receso, Rodríguez volvió a consultar a Salcedo sobre el pedido de extradición en su contra de Estados Unidos. Esta vez, Salcedo aceptó, por lo que se activó el procedimiento expedito para su entrega a ese país.
Compartir:

item.author: Marjorie Ortiz
item.description:
Operativo nocturno con helicóptero en Quito y despliegue policial deja detenidos, armas y droga incautada
2026-09-12
Por Marjorie Ortiz
https://www.primicias.ec/seguridad/helicoptero-policia-quito-detenidos-armas-droga-clausura-bares-132451/
Operativo nocturno con helicóptero en Quito y despliegue policial deja detenidos, armas y droga incautada
El sobrevuelo de helicópteros en la zona del centro y norte de Quito llamó la atención de ciudadanos la noche del 11 de septiembre de 2026, mientras la Policía atribuye operativo al Plan de Protección en la capital.
Imagen que muestra algunos de los productos decomisados durante un operativo de seguridad realizado por la Policía Nacional el viernes 11 de septiembre del 2026
- Foto
API
Autor:
Redacción Primicias
Actualizada:

item.title: Cisma en el correísmo: 37 asambleístas van al Consejo de Disciplina de Revolución Ciudadana por su votación en la Ley de Adopciones
item.author: Roberto Rueda
item.description:
Cisma en el correísmo: 37 asambleístas van al Consejo de Disciplina de Revolución Ciudadana por su votación en la Ley de Adopciones
2026-09-12
Por Roberto Rueda
https://www.primicias.ec/politica/asambleistas-correismo-consejo-disciplina-revolucion-ciudadana-votacion-ley-adopciones-132097/
Cisma en el correísmo: 37 asambleístas van al Consejo de Disciplina de Revolución Ciudadana por su votación en la Ley de Adopciones
La coordinadora de la bancada correísta, Patricia Núñez, los acusa de incumplir una decisión adoptada por órganos directivos. Entre los denunciados están figuras del correísmo, como Viviana Veloz y Ricardo Patiño.
Asambleístas de la bancada de Revolución Ciudadana previo al inicio del debate y aprobación de la Ley de Adopciones el 28 de julio de 2026.
- Foto
Asamblea Nacional.
Autor:
Redacción Primicias
Actualizada:
Compartir:
Un mes y medio después de aprobarse en la Asamblea Nacional la Ley de Adopciones, las repercusiones para los legisladores de la Revolución Ciudadana (RC) que apoyaron la norma del oficialismo podrían empezar.
La coordinadora de la bancada correísta, Patricia Núñez, denunció ante el Consejo de Disciplina y Ética de la organización política a 37 de sus integrantes, entre los que se encuentran Ricardo Patiño, Viviana Veloz y Xavier Lasso.
Los acusa de no haberse acogido a la disciplina del movimiento y desacatar una decisión adoptada en torno a esta normativa que fue aprobada el 28 de julio pasado con el voto de 118 asambleístas, entre ellos, correístas.
¿Cómo se dieron los hechos?
En la bancada de RC existe un equipo de seguimiento jurídico que se encarga de analizar desde el primer momento cada uno de los proyectos de ley que ingresan a la Asamblea Nacional.
Su trabajo consiste en presentar un informe final a la bancada con los puntos a favor, en contra, los que se pueden mejorar y las líneas rojas de la propuesta. Incluye una recomendación de cómo debería votar el correísmo.
En este caso, como en otros, la sugerencia fue que RC no debería apoyar el documento elaborado por la Comisión de Transparencia, que está liderada por Diana Jácome de Acción Democrática Nacional (ADN).
En una sesión virtual, en la que participaron unos 38 legisladores correístas, se tomó la decisión de votar en abstención, lo que habría sido ratificado por la propia presidenta del movimiento, Gabriela Rivadeneira, a través de una llamada telefónica, según pudo conocer PRIMICIAS.
Sin embargo, minutos antes de que se produzca la votación el 28 de julio, algunos asambleístas se acercaron a Nuñez para informarle su voluntad de votar a favor del texto de la Ley de Adopciones impulsado por ADN.
En esta línea se habrían ubicado asambleístas como Pamela Aguirre, Paola Cabezas, Blasco Luna, Luis Molina, Jahiren Noriega, Mónica Palacios, Héctor Rodríguez, Franklin Samaniego, quienes ya fueron notificados.
Eso puso en entredicho el liderazgo de Núñez al interior de la bancada y de la propia Gabriela Rivadeneira como dirigente máxima de la Revolución Ciudadana.
Las posibles sanciones
El Régimen Orgánico del Movimiento Revolución Ciudadana contempla la posibilidad de que sus militantes y adherentes puedan cometer faltas leves y faltas graves.
La faltas leves se sancionan a través de una amonestación escrita y suspensión de los derechos del adherente por un tiempo máximo de seis meses.
En tanto que, si la falta es considerada grave, las sanciones internas en RC pueden ser:
- Suspensión por el tiempo de seis meses a dos años según el alcance de la falta.
- Expulsión definitiva del Movimiento sin perjuicio de sanciones civiles, disciplinarias o penales que dieran lugar.
- Perder el derecho a ser candidata o candidato por el movimiento en el próximo proceso electoral de elección de dignidades y ocupar cargos dentro del movimiento.
"Es un tema interno"
La denuncia presentada por Patricia Núñez ante el Consejo de Disciplina y Ética de la Revolución Ciudadana solo confirma los rumores del malestar al interio
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: El testigo del caso Villavicencio contra José Serrano acepta ser extraditado a Estados Unidos
item.author: Redacción Primicias
item.description:
El testigo del caso Villavicencio contra José Serrano acepta ser extraditado a Estados Unidos
2026-09-12
Por Redacción Primicias
https://www.primicias.ec/politica/rphr-testigo-villavicencio-extradicion-estados-unidos-132170/
El testigo del caso Villavicencio contra José Serrano acepta ser extraditado a Estados Unidos
El exagente de inteligencia RPHR consintió su extradición a Estados Unidos durante la audiencia instalada en la Corte Nacional de Justicia. Se trata de un testigo clave en la causa del magnicidio de Fernando Villavicencio, donde incriminó al exministro José Serrano y a Daniel Salcedo.
Audiencia extradición RPHR el 9 de septiembre de 2026.
- Foto
Captura de la audiencia
Autor:
Actualizada:
Compartir:
Durante la audiencia de extradición pasiva ante la Corte Nacional de Justicia, el exteniente RPHR aceptó, de viva voz, ser entregado a Estados Unidos. El requerido formalizó su consentimiento tras ser consultado por el presidente del organismo, Marco Rodríguez, y confirmar su defensa legal.
RPHR, exagente de inteligencia policial, es testigo clave en el expediente del magnicidio de Fernando Villavicencio. En sus declaraciones, señaló al exministro José Serrano Salgado por ordenar vigilancias y rastreos a la víctima previos al crimen de agosto de 2023.
La jornada en la Corte Nacional continuará esta tarde con la audiencia de extradición de Daniel Salcedo Bonilla. Salcedo, sentenciado en Ecuador por tramas de corrupción, es solicitado por las autoridades estadounidenses dentro de indagaciones por delincuencia transnacional.

item.title: Los carros de Japón están en el top 3 de los más vendidos en Ecuador; estos son los modelos más demandados
item.author: Evelyn Tapia
item.description:
Los carros de Japón están en el top 3 de los más vendidos en Ecuador; estos son los modelos más demandados
2026-09-12
Por Evelyn Tapia
https://www.primicias.ec/economia/ecuador-acuerdo-comercial-japon-carros-japoneses-modelos-132010/
Los carros de Japón están en el top 3 de los más vendidos en Ecuador; estos son los modelos más demandados
El Presidente Daniel Noboa manifestó el interés de Ecuador de buscar un acuerdo comercial con Japón. Si se logra el acuerdo, uno los beneficios podría ser la reducción de aranceles para los carros japoneses.
Imagen referencial de un local de venta de carros japoneses en el norte de Quito, archivo.
- Foto
PRIMICIAS.
Autor:
Redacción Primicias
Actualizada:
Compartir:
Ecuador mira a Japón para un eventual acuerdo comercial. El pasado 4 de septiembre de 2026, el mismo presidente Daniel Noboa reiteró el interés:
"En los últimos 10 años (Japón) se ha vuelto menos competitivo versus Corea y China, y ha visto que sus exportaciones han caído y ya no pueden seguir así. Entonces tienen que abrirse un poco al mundo" lo que implica ampliar importaciones y exportaciones, comentó Noboa.
Aunque todavía no hay información sobre cuándo comenzarían las negociaciones, ya hay expectativas sobre qué productos podrían llegar de Japón con menos aranceles.
Entre los productos con más potencial están los carros, ya que son de los productos que más vende el país nipón a Ecuador; además, Japón es uno de los más grandes competidores en esta industria, explica el economista Gonzalo Cucalón.
Y, además, se ha dado a conocer históricamente por su ingeniería de precisión, alta calidad y precios competitivos, añade Cucalón.
Genaro Baldeón, presidente Ejecutivo de la Asociación de Empresas Automotrices del Ecuador (Aeade), destaca que hay 10 marcas compitiendo en Ecuador, con 38 modelos de origen japonés. De ahí que considera que "un acuerdo comercial ampliaría esa oferta, diversificaría las opciones para el consumidor y permitiría precios más accesibles".
"Japón es el segundo mayor exportador de vehículos del mundo, por lo que un acuerdo con ese origen representaría un impulso significativo para el mercado ecuatoriano"
Genaro Baldeón, Aeade.
Japón está entre los principales países de origen
De los 108.259 carros que se vendieron en Ecuador entre enero y agosto de 2026, unos 6.433 se importaron desde Japón; esto es, el 5,94% del total del mercado, según la Cámara de la Industria Automotriz Ecuatoriana (Cinae).
Las ventas de carros japoneses, además, crecieron 49% entre enero y agosto de 2026 frente a igual período de 2025.
Con este desempeño en lo que va de 2026, Japón ya está en el top tres de principales orígenes de los carros que se venden en Ecuador, como muestra la gráfica:
Los modelos más vendidos
La mayoría de carros que han llegado de Japón a Ecuador en lo que va de 2026 son de la marca de origen estadounidense Chevrolet, que ensambla sobre todo modelos de vehículos pesados en ese país asiático.
Le sigue Mazda, la histórica marca japonesa fundada en Hiroshima en 1920. De hecho, dos modelos de esta marca son los más vendidos de origen japonés hasta agosto: CX30 y CX5, que son del segmento SUV.
Estos son los 10 modelos de carros japoneses más vendidos en Ecuador hasta agosto de 2026:
Japón es, además, un fuerte competidor en el segmento de las tecnologías híbridas, pues es pionero en este mercado.
Fue en el país nipón en donde Toyota lanzó en 1976 un prototipo de carro deportivo híbrido en serie, movido por turbina de gas y un motor eléctrico. Se llamaba el Toyota GT Hybrid Concept, basado en el Toyota Sports 800 de 1969.
Para finales de 1990, Toyota lanzó el modelo híbrido Prius, que es el primer vehículo híbrido de fabricación masiva.
Gremios tienen expectativas por el acuerdo
Baldeón destaca que un acuerdo comercial permitiría que la participación crezca. Aeade representa a varias empresas importadoras de vehículos.
"Con la Unión Europea, la participación de mercado pasó del 2% en 2016
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: SpaceX signs another AI computing deal, with $100 billion in ARR 'on track,' CFO says
item.author: Pras Subramanian
item.description:
SpaceX signs another AI computing deal, with $100 billion in ARR 'on track,' CFO says
2026-09-12
Por Pras Subramanian
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/spacex-signs-another-ai-computing-deal-with-100-billion-in-arr-on-track-cfo-says-152933886.html
SpaceX (SPCX) just inked another big AI compute deal, one that will take the space and rocket company closer to its $100 billion annual recurring revenue (ARR) target this year, a big metric for investors.
At the Goldman Sachs Communacopia & Technology Conference in San Francisco, CFO Bret Johnsen said a new AI compute deal has been reached in which SpaceX leases out compute bandwidth for third-party clients.
"We're on track, or we believe we're on track to hit $100 billion ARR," Johnsen said about SpaceX's overall ARR target, as AI compute deals helped fuel the growth, before revealing the news. "What I would tell you, an update to that is that just earlier this month we closed another hosting deal, and that translates into about $1.11 billion a month starting December 1st of this year, which is another roughly $13 billion of ARR."
Add this to deals already in place, and SpaceX's compute deals are creating a nice revenue stream. Earlier this year, SpaceX announced a compute deal with Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) for $1.25 billion per month ($15 billion ARR) and another deal with Alphabet's (GOOG, GOOGL) Google for $920 million per month ($11.04 billion ARR).
In a note to clients, William Blair analyst Louie DiPalma confirmed that the new deal differs from the $6.7 billion, six-month deal ($13.4 billion ARR) that was announced on SpaceX's August earnings call. "We suspect the $6.7 billion/6-month deal that was announced on the earnings call is with the U.S. Department of Defense," he said.
DiPalma explained why SpaceX is winning with its AI compute business.
"SpaceX has benefited from its ability to deploy capacity much faster than peers to take advantage of the unprecedented demand environment for compute capacity," DiPalma said. "In addition, SpaceX has benefited from its close relationship with Nvidia, which provides SpaceXAI with priority allocation to GPUs."
The four deals noted here — without mentioning any other deals SpaceX has in place — amount to around $45.7 billion in ARR for December. Add the rocket business (approximately $4 billion in ARR based on Q2 earnings) and the Starlink division ($17.2 billion), and it seems possible that $100 billion could be reached as growth continues, with Johnsen saying he has "even more conviction" in hitting that goal.
One wrinkle in its AI compute game plan is that SpaceX is now considering slowing the physical build-outs of its terrestrial data centers to help address operational and reliability concerns, per The Information.

"What I would tell you, an update to that is that just earlier this month we closed another hosting deal, and that translates into about $1.11 billion a month starting December 1st of this year, which is another roughly $13 billion of ARR."
Add this to deals already in place, and SpaceX's compute deals are creating a nice revenue stream. Earlier this year, SpaceX announced a compute deal with Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) for $1.25 billion per month ($15 billion ARR) and another deal with Alphabet's (GOOG, GOOGL) Google for $920 million per month ($11.04 billion ARR).
In a note to clients, William Blair analyst Louie DiPalma confirmed that the new deal differs from the $6.7 billion, six-month deal ($13.4 billion ARR) that was announced on SpaceX's August earnings call. "We suspect the $6.7 billion/6-month deal that was announced on the earnings call is with the U.S. Department of Defense," he said.
DiPalma explained why SpaceX is winning with its AI compute business.
"SpaceX has benefited from its ability to deploy capacity much faster than peers to take advantage of the unprecedented demand environment for compute capacity," DiPalma said. "In addition, SpaceX has benefited from its close relationship with Nvidia, which provides SpaceXAI with priority allocation to GPUs."
The four deals noted here — without mentioning any other deals SpaceX has in place — amount to around $45.7 billion in ARR for December. Add the rocket business (approximately $4 billion in ARR based on Q2 earnings) and the Starlink division ($17.2 billion), and it seems possible that $100 billion could be reached as growth continues, with Johnsen saying he has "even more conviction" in hitting that goal.
One wrinkle in its AI compute game plan is that SpaceX is now considering slowing the physical build-outs of its terrestrial data centers to help address operational and reliability concerns, per The Information.

item.title: Anthropic Says US Adversaries Aimed Claude at Weapons Research
item.author: Olivia Solon; Jordan Robertson; Ryan Gallagher
item.description:
Anthropic Says US Adversaries Aimed Claude at Weapons Research
2026-09-12
Por Olivia Solon; Jordan Robertson; Ryan Gallagher
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/anthropic-says-us-adversaries-aimed-120427318.html
(Bloomberg) -- Anthropic PBC says its artificial intelligence model Claude has been misused in attempts to develop a wide range of potential military applications, including kamikaze drone swarms, missile navigation systems and biological weapons.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Users from countries including Iran, Russia, China and Yemen are among those flagged for misusing the AI company's frontier models in the past year, according to a report by Anthropic's threat intelligence team on Thursday. None of the cases involved Anthropic's most advanced models, Fable and Mythos.
"As models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society's defenders act to make them safer," Anthropic said in the report.
US AI companies have been racing to develop and deploy more capable AI systems, in part to stay ahead of rivals like China, while trying to maintain safeguards. Anthropic is seeking to prevent its technology from being used for harmful purposes, including the development of biological and conventional weapons.
That position brought it into direct conflict with the Pentagon, which suspended work with Anthropic after it refused to allow Claude to be used for mass surveillance or autonomous weapons systems.
The report says users have attempted to deploy Claude to help America's enemies. In many cases they tried to evade Claude's safeguards or conceal their locations.
Users in Russia, which Anthropic determined were not linked to the state, tried to use Claude to build software for an autonomous, first-person-view, kamikaze drone swarm trained on Ukrainian combat footage.
The report also details five case studies of people using Claude in ways that could support the development of biological weapons, including state-sponsored virologists looking to create an enhanced version of a debilitating mosquito-borne virus called chikungunya. The effort was identified through a request for Claude to help write a grant application to fund research at a military institute in an unnamed country where Anthropic doesn't provide service.
Anthropic noted that all of the biological case studies in the report were "ambiguous" and involved research that could have benign scientific intent.
Actors based in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen, however, used Claude to build software for several types of missiles.
"We do not have evidence the actors succeeded in fielding an operational device," Anthropic said.
State-linked actors in countries including China and Iran tried to use Claude to build and facilitate surveillance. One China-linked operation used Claude to "track, profile and recruit Uyghurs" in the Syrian Army. An Iranian unit used Claude to build surveillance software disguised as a tool to keep track of prayer times. China's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In another case, it discovered that a consultant likely working for a state intelligence agency in Mali had used Claude to build a system designed to monitor roughly 25 million mobile phones in the West African country. The system could generate "intelligence dossiers" on any specified phone number, without a court order. Anthropic said that it banned the consultant's account, but that the Claude-powered surveillance platform had been deployed locally and was out of the company's full control. The Malian government did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Anthropic's report also highlighted how hackers — ranging from suspected state-sponsored intelligence in Russia and China to hacktivists and cybercriminals — are using the company's AI to speed up and amplify their efforts to steal sensitive data. The report does not reveal any novel or dangerous new vulnerabilities in criti
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: Fed’s Rate Decision May Have Come Down to Phone Plan Changes
item.author: Jeffrey Sparshott; Matthew Boesler
item.description:
Fed’s Rate Decision May Have Come Down to Phone Plan Changes
2026-09-12
Por Jeffrey Sparshott; Matthew Boesler
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/fed-rate-decision-may-come-154304847.html
(Bloomberg) -- A record jump in the price of cellular phone services helped tip a key measure of US inflation above forecasts, likely sealing the deal for a Federal Reserve interest-rate increase next week.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The consumer price index excluding food and energy climbed 0.3% in August from a month earlier, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data out Friday. The median estimate in a Bloomberg survey called for a 0.2% increase. The 5.9% surge in wireless telephone services prices alone added about a 10th of a percentage point to the core reading.
That gauge largely reflects prepaid and monthly plans offered by cellular carriers.
Economists at Bank of America Corp., Barclays Plc and Pantheon Macroeconomics flagged recent plan changes by major carriers like AT&T Inc. and T-Mobile US Inc. as likely culprits. The BLS declined to elaborate on how the changes at those carriers may have impacted the number.
AT&T said earlier this year that it would implement price increases on certain plans in August. T-Mobile also recently retired some of its legacy plans, resulting in price increases for consumers.
Even so, many Fed-watchers still saw a case for raising interest rates, even if underlying inflation was lifted last month partly by one-time factors.
"While it is true that the wireless index added 10bps to the core CPI today, and that the core ex-wireless would have been 0.20%, I don't think the Fed will have the luxury of slicing and dicing the data at the meeting next week," Omair Sharif, president of Inflation Insights LLC, said in a note.
--With assistance from Kelcee Griffis.
Most Read from Bloomberg Businessweek
2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: Trump’s ‘Golden Age’ Confronts Economic Angst That Threatens GOP
item.author: Josh Wingrove
item.description:
Trump’s ‘Golden Age’ Confronts Economic Angst That Threatens GOP
2026-09-12
Por Josh Wingrove
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/trump-golden-age-confronts-economic-173000047.html
(Bloomberg) -- The Republican faithful, gathered in arena hallways and hotel ballrooms during this week's midterm convention, projected confidence they had a good story to tell on the economy.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Some pointed to the steady unemployment rate and stock market growth as evidence of a new "Golden Age" driven by a resilient economy and American consumer, while others argued immigration and manufacturing policies were yielding a better life for US citizens.
Still, a latent anxiety hung over Dallas. The reality — that polls suggest voters are in fact quite anxious about the state of the economy, and preparing to punish Republicans in November's midterm elections — has become hard for even President Donald Trump to ignore.
Ultimately, the way voters feel about an economy that is a mess of contradictions - growing and stable but expensive and inequitable — seems likely to dictate the results of the vote, and, consequently, how much longer Trump can single-handedly reshape the federal government.
Fuel prices are surging up, despite the end of the summer travel season. Data out Friday showed little progress on inflation last month, which investors and economists say will likely lead the Federal Reserve to hike rates next week over Trump's public objections.
Consumer sentiment slid below estimates in September, with consumers expecting prices will continue to rise. Just 35% of Republicans in the University of Michigan survey believe the government is doing a good job with the economy, the lowest reading since Trump returned to the White House last year.
Peppered throughout the president's celebration of his second-term accomplishments was a growing, albeit, tacit admission of needing to do more to reassure voters: by acknowledging some victories could take time to manifest, and by dangling the prospect of a $5,000 "Trump dividend." Pressed as he departed the convention on why such a payment was necessary if the economy was thriving, Trump told reporters he intended it as a "reward" for those who had suffered during President Joe Biden's presidency. But he allowed that conditions hadn't immediately improved upon his taking office.
"They had to put up with the four years, and that carried on at least half an additional year," Trump said.
Vice President JD Vance's keynote Thursday nodded to outrage over housing costs, imploring Republican voters to stick with the party even if they don't agree on everything. US 30-year mortgage rates climbed to a one-year high earlier this week; prior to the Iran war, costs for home borrowing had fallen to their lowest level since 2022.
Trump was an inescapable presence over the two nights, speaking twice from the stage, sitting for a Fox News interview, chatting with traveling reporters and hosting high-dollar fundraisers.
He insisted to all that would listen that things were good.
Growth, Trump argued in a Fox News interview, could not only pay for his $1.2 trillion dividend giveaway but help address a national debt that in recent weeks has surpassed $40 trillion, roiling the bond market. Inflation is elevated, but not nearly as high as seen during the Biden administration. The extension of his signature tax cut law — and new provisions giving seniors an additional break and removing federal taxes on some tips — meant tax returns were higher. Prescription drug prices have in some cases ticked down.
"We've had record employment in this country," said Ray Washburne, the Sunoco LP chairman who co-chaired the committee staging the convention in Dallas. "We're having boom times in a market like this, and I think that shows the rest of the country what can be done."
But framing the economy as humming along is a risky gamble.
While the Internal Revenue Service issued roughly 99 million re

item.title: Rising Bond Yields Are Driving US Stocks Toward Correction Territory: Markets Pulse
item.author: Kerry Benn
item.description:
Rising Bond Yields Are Driving US Stocks Toward Correction Territory: Markets Pulse
2026-09-12
Por Kerry Benn
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/rising-bond-yields-driving-us-093100638.html
(Bloomberg) -- The escalating bond selloff is driving US Treasury yields toward levels that threaten to deal a significant blow to the stock market, according to the latest Markets Pulse survey.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Around 30% of the 122 people who responded to the poll by Bloomberg said 10-year yields hitting 5% to 5.25% would be enough to set off a 10% drop in stocks from their peak, a decline that would meet the definition of a correction. 22% pegged the range slightly higher, at 5.25% to 5.5%.
The benchmark 10-year yield climbed on Thursday to over 4.96%, a fresh three-year high, as the conflict President Donald Trump unleashed in the Middle East pushed oil well over $100 a barrel, raising the specter of a worsening inflation shock and a response from the Federal Reserve.
"One would think that we are on the cusp of a long-anticipated correction in the equity market as actual data and central bank policy provide a potent reality check for risk-loving investors," said Joseph Brusuelas, RSM chief economist.
The Treasury rate, a key benchmark for the cost of money in the wider economy and the valuation of equities, has already sparked concern in the Trump administration with November's midterm elections nearing. Survey participants cited accelerating price pressures and fiscal concerns as the top threats to Treasuries over the next six months.
The key yield has climbed a full percentage point since Trump starting bombing Iran at the end of February and is hovering just below the roughly 5% peak last hit in late 2023, after the Fed wrapped up the interest-rate hikes aimed at taming the post-pandemic inflation surge.
The latest rise is coming instead as traders brace for the Fed to start raising rates again as soon as next week, with new Chairman Kevin Warsh under pressure to show he's prepared to act on his pledge to rein in inflation that's held over the bank's target since 2021.
If Warsh does lead the Fed in a hike, more than 80% of survey participants think that will be part of a one- or two-time mid-cycle adjustment rather than the beginning of a larger series of increases.
A steady stream of solid earnings reports have so far overshadowed the impact of higher rates, with the S&P 500 Index not far below last month's record highs despite a 2% slide over the past four days.

The benchmark 10-year yield climbed on Thursday to over 4.96%, a fresh three-year high, as the conflict President Donald Trump unleashed in the Middle East pushed oil well over $100 a barrel, raising the specter of a worsening inflation shock and a response from the Federal Reserve.

"One would think that we are on the cusp of a long-anticipated correction in the equity market as actual data and central bank policy provide a potent reality check for risk-loving investors," said Joseph Brusuelas, RSM chief economist.

The Treasury rate, a key benchmark for the cost of money in the wider economy and the valuation of equities, has already sparked concern in the Trump administration with November's midterm elections nearing. Survey participants cited accelerating price pressures and fiscal concerns as the top threats to Treasuries over the next six months.

The key yield has climbed a full percentage point since Trump starting bombing Iran at the end of February and is hovering just below the roughly 5% peak last hit in late 2023, after the Fed wrapped up the interest-rate hikes aimed at taming the post-pandemic inflation surge.

The latest rise is coming instead as traders brace for the Fed to start raising rates again as soon as next week, with new Chairman Kevin Warsh under pressure to show he's prepared to act on his pledge to rein in inflation that's held over the bank's target since 2021.

If Warsh does lead the Fed in a hike, more than 80% of survey participants think that will be part of a one- or two-time mid-cycle adjustment rather than the beginning of a larger series of increases.

A steady stream of solid earnings reports have so far overshadowed the impact of higher rates, with the S&P 500 Index not far below last month's record highs despite a 2% slide over the past four days.

item.title: Global Bond Selloff Sends 10-Year Treasury Yields to Cusp of 5%
item.author: Cameron Fozi; Greg Ritchie
item.description:
Global Bond Selloff Sends 10-Year Treasury Yields to Cusp of 5%
2026-09-12
Por Cameron Fozi; Greg Ritchie
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/global-bond-selloff-sends-10-001324539.html
(Bloomberg) -- Bond bears are pushing benchmark Treasury yields toward the closely-watched 5% level ahead of US inflation data that stands to determine expectations for a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike next week.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The yield on 10-year notes climbed 18 basis points this week to trade just below the psychologically-important level, which may attract dip buyers but also risks triggering further selling that could spill over into global markets. At 4.96% on Friday, the yield has reached the most-elevated level since 2023 — and is approaching its highest since 2007.
The surge in yields comes as traders wrestle with rising oil prices and inflation that's run above the Federal Reserve's target for half a decade. A reading of the US consumer price index Friday stands to be one of the most pivotal in years as traders price in a roughly 70% chance of a rate increase at the Sept. 16 Fed meeting.
"Hitting 5% on the 10-year Treasury yield looks more like an inevitability here than a forecast," said Padhraic Garvey, head of research for the Americas at ING Groep NV. "These are worrying times for bond markets."
Yields on the two-year, which are more sensitive to Fed rate moves, rose to as high as 4.59% this week. Thirty-year yields hit their highest since 2007, luring standout demand at an auction of the securities.
The moves have spilled over into bond markets worldwide, with Australian benchmark yields hitting their highest since 2011 on Friday and Japanese equivalents trading close to the key psychological level of 3%. A gauge of global yields is at its highest since 2007.
"A lower US CPI and a Fed hike are really the only circuit breakers I see at this point, otherwise I don't think anyone is comfortable being long rates," said Michael Tang, a rates strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia in Sydney. "It's just massive hawkish sentiment taking over."
That leaves traders on edge going into Friday's main economic event — especially as Fed officials have underscored their focus on inflation in recent weeks. To Molly Brooks, a US rates strategist at TD Securities, a hotter-than-expected print stands to boost market expectations for a hike in September and additional tightening.

item.title: Trump said he'll stop Canada's Bombardier from being sold in the US
item.author: Aditi Bharade
item.description:
Trump said he'll stop Canada's Bombardier from being sold in the US
2026-09-11
Por Aditi Bharade
https://businessinsider.com/trump-stop-canada-bombardier-sold-us-2026-9
President Donald Trump doesn't want one particular Canadian aircraft crossing over into the US.
In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump wrote: "No more selling Bombardier in the United States! Their products aren't good enough."
Trump said that if the company wants business from the US, it needs to build its jets in the US. Bombardier, an aircraft manufacturer based in Montreal, makes business and private luxury jets.
US federal agencies such as the US Air Force and the Federal Aviation Administration were previously reported to have Bombardier aircraft in their fleets. Representatives for the White House did not respond to a query from Business Insider on whether any federal agencies are canceling orders with Bombardier after Trump's announcement.
Bombardier wrote in a statement on its website on Monday, without any reference to Trump's post, that it's a "strong contributor" to the American aerospace industry, creating "tens of thousands of jobs across the United States."
The statement said that Bombardier's American workers are based across the US, with sites in Kansas, Texas, Arizona, Florida, Connecticut, Illinois, Delaware, California, Washington, D.C., and New Jersey. It has "overall direct employment presence in more than 20 states," Bombardier said.
The company said it also uses American-made aircraft components in its manufacturing, like engines, wings, and avionics. Its supply chain includes 2,800 American companies across 47 states, it added.
"Bombardier values its great partnership with American companies and its U.S. employees," the company said in the statement. "Our plan is to continue to invest in our people, our customers, and the communities in which we operate across the country."
Trump's post comes as trade tensions between the two neighbors flare. Canada's latest round of tariffs went into effect on Tuesday, imposing 50% duties on hundreds of US goods, including cheese, honey, and aluminum foil. These levies are a retaliatory response to the 50% tariffs the US imposed on Canadian products such as dairy, alcohol, and electronics.

item.title: US consumer sentiment deteriorates in September, inflation expectations rise
item.author: Reuters
item.description:
US consumer sentiment deteriorates in September, inflation expectations rise
2026-09-11
Por Reuters
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/us-consumer-sentiment-deteriorates-september-142448698.html
WASHINGTON, Sept 11 (Reuters) - U.S. consumer sentiment deteriorated in early September as rising gasoline prices and trade tensions stoked fears of higher inflation over the next 12 months, a survey showed on Friday.
The University of Michigan's Surveys of Consumers said its Consumer Sentiment Index dropped to 47.8 this month from 51.7 in August. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the index at 51,0. Sentiment sagged among consumers identifying as Democrats and Republicans, but was little changed among Independents.
"With a resurgence in fuel prices and trade tensions, consumers anticipate greater pressures on their pocketbooks to come," said Joanne Hsu, the director of the Surveys of Consumers.
The survey's measure of consumer expectations for inflation over the next year jumped to 4.6% from 4.0% last month. Twelve-month inflation expectations were at 3.4% in February before the U.S.-led war with Iran started. Consumers' expectations for inflation over the next five years edged up 3.4% from 3.3% in August. They are higher than their 2024 range of 2.8% to 3.2%.
(Reporting By Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama )

item.title: US diesel prices cross $6 per gallon, setting new record
item.author: Jake Conley
item.description:
US diesel prices cross $6 per gallon, setting new record
2026-09-11
Por Jake Conley
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/us-diesel-prices-cross-6-per-gallon-setting-new-record-122447671.html
US diesel prices crossed the $6 per gallon mark on Friday for the first time on record, setting a new all-time high as global conflict has roiled the energy complex and sent prices of oil products soaring.
The diesel price paid at the pump was $6.05 per gallon on Friday, per AAA, a startlingly fast climb up from $5.32 one month ago and $3.70 a year ago. Prices on the leading crude benchmarks, international Brent (BZ=F) and US WTI (CL=F), both remained up roughly 20% over the past month, even after pulling back by several percentage points overnight.
Diesel prices, especially, are closely watched due to the fuel's role as the "workhorse" of the global economy, powering everything from US 18-wheeler trucks to home heaters in the US Northeast, hospital generators, and construction equipment.
Prices on the entire energy complex have soared since the US and Israel began striking Iran in late February, kicking off the largest and longest-lasting war in the Middle East since the Gulf wars of the early 2000s. As Tehran's military forces moved to cut off oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, the world's most critical chokepoint for energy supplies, crude oil prices soared, pushing toward $120 per barrel.
Read more: How oil price shocks ripple through your wallet, from gas to groceries
Yet the surge in pricing on refined products made from crude oil — such as diesel, gasoline, and jet fuel — has moved up faster and more firmly.
Even as exports of crude from the Persian Gulf have recovered to roughly two-thirds of their pre-war levels, per Goldman Sachs, refining capacity around the world remains severely limited, and supplies remain at years-long lows.
Strikes by Iran and Yemen-based Houthi militants have affected refining infrastructure throughout the Gulf region. To the north, Ukraine's drone strikes have proven highly effective at damaging refineries inside Russia, which supplied roughly 10% of global diesel exports prior to Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Vladimir Putin's government implemented an export ban on diesel to safeguard domestic demand in July and extended that ban through the end of September.
Major US and international refiners disclosed in recent earnings reports that they are running their refineries at near-100% capacity. Such fullness in refinery runs has put the energy market in a situation where, even if more crude oil is brought to market, there aren't refiners available to turn that crude into the products that are actually used to power the global economy.

item.title: Hassett Says Trump $5,000 Checks Can Be Fiscally Responsible
item.author: Michael Sasso
item.description:
Hassett Says Trump $5,000 Checks Can Be Fiscally Responsible
2026-09-11
Por Michael Sasso
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/hassett-says-trump-5-000-145221110.html
(Bloomberg) -- White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett played down concerns that President Donald Trump's proposal to send $5,000 checks to every adult US citizen would add to worries about historically high government borrowing.
Most Read from Bloomberg
"We can do it in a fiscally responsible way," Hassett said in an interview Thursday with Bloomberg TV. "It is a serious proposal."
He argued that "because of all the growth and all the wealth being created in the US, the president thinks we need to return more of that to the American people." He said one way of doing that is via a reconciliation bill — a legislative mechanism that the majority party in the House and Senate can use for a fiscal package that bypasses the need for votes from the opposing party.
When pressed on what sort of offsets might be twinned with the checks — which would amount to more than $1 trillion in added spending at a time the US federal debt burden is heading toward a record high — Hassett said that would have to be "negotiated with Congress."
Trump floated the $5,000 proposal earlier this week, conditional on Republicans retaining their congressional majorities.
Fed Hike?
"The bottom line is there are multiple paths to getting it done — don't underestimate President Trump," Hassett said.
Analysts are skeptical the $5,000 payments will come to fruition, after top GOP lawmakers in the House and Senate offered a muted reaction to the idea.
"President Trump's attention-grabbing proposal for $5,000 checks to all adults if Republicans win the midterms is a non-starter in Congress, due to the massive fiscal cost and inflationary impacts," Evercore ISI analysts wrote in a note Friday.
The NEC director also on Friday said that while the August consumer price index release showed an acceleration in prices, the three-month trend still shows a deceleration in inflation. Asked about the potential for the Federal Reserve to react by raising interest rates next week, Hassett said, "I would guess that if the Fed makes a big move, the president will have something to say about it."
--With assistance from Vonnie Quinn and Michael McKee.
Most Read from Bloomberg Businessweek

item.content:encoded:
Hassett Says Trump $5,000 Checks Can Be Fiscally Responsible

2026-09-11

Por Michael Sasso

https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/hassett-says-trump-5-000-145221110.html

(Bloomberg) -- White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett played down concerns that President Donald Trump's proposal to send $5,000 checks to every adult US citizen would add to worries about historically high government borrowing.

Most Read from Bloomberg

"We can do it in a fiscally responsible way," Hassett said in an interview Thursday with Bloomberg TV. "It is a serious proposal."

He argued that "because of all the growth and all the wealth being created in the US, the president thinks we need to return more of that to the American people." He said one way of doing that is via a reconciliation bill — a legislative mechanism that the majority party in the House and Senate can use for a fiscal package that bypasses the need for votes from the opposing party.

When pressed on what sort of offsets might be twinned with the checks — which would amount to more than $1 trillion in added spending at a time the US federal debt burden is heading toward a record high — Hassett said that would have to be "negotiated with Congress."

Trump floated the $5,000 proposal earlier this week, conditional on Republicans retaining their congressional majorities.

Fed Hike?

"The bottom line is there are multiple paths to getting it done — don't underestimate President Trump," Hassett said.

Analysts are skeptical the $5,000 payments will come to fruition, after top GOP lawmakers in the House and Senate offered a muted reaction to the idea.

"President Trump's attention-grabbing proposal for $5,000 checks to all adults if Republicans win the midterms is a non-starter in Congress, due to the massive fiscal cost and inflationary impacts," Evercore ISI analysts wrote in a note Friday.

The NEC director also on Friday said that while the August consumer price index release showed an acceleration in prices, the three-month trend still shows a deceleration in inflation. Asked about the potential for the Federal Reserve to react by raising interest rates next week, Hassett said, "I would guess that if the Fed makes a big move, the president will have something to say about it."

--With assistance from Vonnie Quinn and Michael McKee.

Most Read from Bloomberg Businessweek

item.title: Consumer sentiment falls as rising gas prices weigh on wallets, inflation expectations tick up
item.author: Grace O'Donnell
item.description:
Consumer sentiment falls as rising gas prices weigh on wallets, inflation expectations tick up
2026-09-11
Por Grace O'Donnell
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/consumer-sentiment-falls-as-rising-gas-prices-weigh-on-wallets-inflation-expectations-tick-up-160440898.html
Consumers report feeling more dour about the US economy as rising gas prices and trade tensions weigh on personal finances and business outlooks, according to a new survey from the University of Michigan.
A preliminary reading showed consumer sentiment fell to 47.8 this month, down from 51.7 in August and below economists' expectations of 51. The gauge marked the second consecutive month of worsening sentiment.
Read more: What is consumer confidence, and why does it matter?
Notably, inflation expectations for the next 12 months jumped to 4.6% from 4% last month, increasing to the highest level since June. Longer-run inflation expectations also edged higher to 3.4%.
"With a resurgence in fuel prices and trade tensions, consumers anticipate greater pressures on their pocketbooks to come," survey director Joanne Hsu said.
The survey's results came after the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) report showed prices remained sticky in August, rising 0.4% month over month and 3.4% year over year, driven by higher energy costs.
The war in Iran and the subsequent surge in energy prices have taken a toll on how consumers feel about the economy. After hitting a record low in May, sentiment remains 16% below where it was in February, before the conflict in the Middle East began.
Rising gas prices, in particular, have been a key concern that consumers have raised this year as they confront higher fuel costs plastered on towering gas station signs. The cost of gas spiked 3.9% last month as the war in Iran rekindled, and Americans now pay an average of $4.28 a gallon at the pump, according to GasBuddy.
Despite reporting more pessimistic attitudes about economic conditions, Americans continue to spend. They also plan to keep spending at similar levels as last year this holiday season.

item.title: Fed rate hike odds surge to 90% on monthly jump in core prices
item.author: Jennifer Schonberger
item.description:
Fed rate hike odds surge to 90% on monthly jump in core prices
2026-09-11
Por Jennifer Schonberger
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article/fed-rate-hike-odds-surge-to-90-on-monthly-jump-in-core-prices-131206510.html
A fresh reading on inflation showed monthly prices rose more than expected in August, increasing the likelihood the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next week.
Stripping out volatile food and energy prices — the way the Fed likes to scrutinize underlying inflation — the Consumer Price Index rose 0.3% month over month, compared with expectations for 0.2%. The year-over-year rate was in line with expectations for 2.4% and down a tenth of a percentage point from July. On a headline basis, CPI rose 3.4% in August, in line with expectations, and 0.4% month over month.
"The upside surprise to core CPI in August means the Fed looks set to hike next week," said Stephen Brown, North America chief economist for Capital Economics.
Markets are now betting on a 90% chance of a rate hike at Wednesday's Fed policy meeting, according to CME FedWatch.
Officials will use the latest inflation data to examine trends over the past three, six, and 12 months to assess whether price pressures are easing.
Fed officials have been divided about whether inflation is falling back down to their 2% goal on its own or whether they need to raise rates. Friday's data will fuel hawks like Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack and Dallas Fed president Lorie Logan, who argue that inflation is broad-based and that without increasing rates, it won't come down on its own.
It may also not be enough to satisfy officials like Fed governor Chris Waller, who said last week that if August figures show inflation coming down and core prices staying at 0.2%, he would support holding rates steady next week.
"If there is continued progress toward our 2% goal, then I am willing to support holding the policy rate at its current level," Waller said on Sept. 3. "But if inflation comes in hot, I would consider a rate hike. I judge that policy is currently only slightly restricting aggregate demand, and it may not take much acceleration in inflation to nudge me into supporting tighter policy."
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said in a speech at Jackson Hole, Wyo., last month that inflation is too high and that rates are not restricting borrowing in the economy, outside of housing. He noted that June and July inflation readings, which had shown some progress, hadn't been enough for him to mark the improvement he needs to see that inflation is coming down.
"Following a brief easing in June and July, inflation surged again in August which sets the stage for a likely interest rate hike," RSM chief economist Joseph Brusuelas said. He expects the Fed to hike at least two more times after next week over the next year to put inflation on a credible path back to 2%.
New York Fed president John Williams has said that if monthly readings on inflation consistently came in at 0.2% on the Personal Consumption Expenditures index (PCE) — another inflation measure and the Fed's favored yardstick — then that would indicate inflation is coming down.
Fed officials will use CPI along with data on wholesale prices released Thursday to back into estimates for PCE.
Capital Economics economist Brown estimates core PCE rose by 0.27% month over month in August, with that figure unlikely to be much affected by the forthcoming revisions to the portfolio management and software and accessories price calculations. Without taking those revisions into account, that monthly estimate implies that annual core PCE inflation would rise from 3.3% in July to 3.4%.
"In short, core PCE inflation is moving in the wrong direction, and that should be enough for the centrists on the FOMC such as Governor Christopher Waller to support a hike next week," Brown said.

item.title: US consumer prices accelerate in August, push Fed closer to rate hike
item.author: Lucia Mutikani
item.description:
US consumer prices accelerate in August, push Fed closer to rate hike
2026-09-11
Por Lucia Mutikani
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/us-consumer-inflation-picks-august-123741290.html
US consumer prices accelerate in August, push Fed closer to rate hike
By Lucia Mutikani
6 min read
By Lucia Mutikani
WASHINGTON, Sept 11 (Reuters) - U.S. consumer prices accelerated in August, while a key measure of underlying inflation posted its largest increase in four months, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next week.
The Labor Department's Consumer Price Index report on Friday followed strong readings in several components of the Producer Price Index released on Thursday that feed into the Personal Consumption Expenditures price indexes, the inflation measures the U.S. central bank tracks for its 2% target. The two reports led economists to think that PCE inflation excluding the volatile food and energy categories picked up in August.
Financial markets initially priced in a 91% chance of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday, before settling back to 87%, CME's FedWatch tool showed. That was up from 72% on Thursday. The Fed's benchmark overnight interest rate is currently in a 3.50%-3.75% range.
Most economists said the firmer inflation readings, combined with signs of the labor market regaining its footing in August, would compel Fed officials to raise borrowing costs not only next Wednesday, but possibly again in October or December.
They argued that with the Iran war continuing, the energy shock would spread through the economy. They also expected an AI buildout to drive inflation. Crude oil prices climbed back above $100 a barrel this week, while the U.S. national average diesel price surpassed $6 a gallon for the first time.
"Energy inflation does not stay at the gas station. It travels by truck, airplane and cargo ship into nearly every store in America," said Sung Won Sohn, a finance and economics professor at Loyola Marymount University. "The Fed is now more likely than not to raise its policy rate ... it cannot afford to let an energy shock become an everything shock."
The CPI increased 0.4% last month after edging up 0.1% in July, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said. In the 12 months through August, consumer inflation advanced 3.4% after rising by the same margin in July. The rise in the CPI was in line with economists' expectations.
A 3.9% jump in gasoline prices after two straight monthly declines accounted for more than a third of the increase in the CPI over the month. Other motor fuels, which include diesel, surged 9.6%. They surged 44% year-on-year in August.
There was, however, some respite for consumers at the supermarket. Food prices edged up 0.1% for a second straight month. Grocery prices were unchanged amid muted increases in the costs of meat and fish. Fruit and vegetable prices fell 0.4% over the month, weighed down by a 6.2% drop in the cost of lettuce because of a Cyclospora outbreak.
But egg prices increased 2.9%, while nonalcoholic beverages cost more, as did dairy and related products. Food prices advanced 2.7% year-on-year in August and the annual increase in consumer inflation is outpacing wage growth. Inflation-adjusted average hourly earnings fell 0.3% over the year in August.
"Inflation-adjusted wage growth contracted for a fifth consecutive month in August," said Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon. "This is the longest income squeeze since 2012 – excluding the post-pandemic period when public assistance kept income growing despite historical job losses."
FRUSTRATION OVER RISING COST OF LIVING
Frustration over the higher cost of living has led to a sharp erosion in President Donald Trump's approval ratings and could cost his Republican Party control of the U.S. Congress in the November midterm elections, according to analysts.
The growing disenchantment was also evid
[Transcripcion recortada]

Grocery prices were unchanged amid muted increases in the costs of meat and fish. Fruit and vegetable prices fell 0.4% over the month, weighed down by a 6.2% drop in the cost of lettuce because of a Cyclospora outbreak.
But egg prices increased 2.9%, while nonalcoholic beverages cost more, as did dairy and related products. Food prices advanced 2.7% year-on-year in August and the annual increase in consumer inflation is outpacing wage growth. Inflation-adjusted average hourly earnings fell 0.3% over the year in August.
"Inflation-adjusted wage growth contracted for a fifth consecutive month in August," said Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon. "This is the longest income squeeze since 2012 – excluding the post-pandemic period when public assistance kept income growing despite historical job losses."
FRUSTRATION OVER RISING COST OF LIVING
Frustration over the higher cost of living has led to a sharp erosion in President Donald Trump's approval ratings and could cost his Republican Party control of the U.S. Congress in the November midterm elections, according to analysts.

item.title: 'We intend to be disruptive': Robinhood CEO details big investment bank ambitions after Oura IPO win
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
'We intend to be disruptive': Robinhood CEO details big investment bank ambitions after Oura IPO win
2026-09-11
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/we-intend-to-be-disruptive-robinhood-ceo-details-big-investment-bank-ambitions-after-oura-ipo-win-151806118.html
'We intend to be disruptive': Robinhood CEO details big investment bank ambitions after Oura IPO win
SAN FRANCISCO, Calif. — Robinhood (HOOD) appears to be grabbing a piece of lucrative underwriting business from old-school investment banks.
The company officially landed its first-ever formal IPO underwriting role, joining a syndicate of 18 institutions listed on smart-ring maker Oura's recent S-1 filing.
While Wall Street giants like Goldman Sachs (GS), Morgan Stanley (MS), and JPMorgan Chase (JPM) are acting as lead bookrunners, the inclusion of Robinhood (No. 18 on the underwriting list) gives it stronger leverage over share allocations for its massive retail trading user base.
"We want to do more," Robinhood co-founder and CEO Vlad Tenev told Yahoo Finance from the Goldman Sachs Communacopia & Tech Conference (video above). "I think as an underwriter we'll really be able to represent retail and be in the room in a big way, which will hopefully lead to bigger allocations."
It also cements Robinhood's efforts to become a one-stop shop for wealth management services. That push has seen Robinhood venture into prediction markets and accrue more than $3 billion in banking deposits.
"We have been offering retail investors access to IPOs for many years now," Tenev added. "It's always been as what's called a selling group member. What that means is we're distributing shares on behalf of the underwriters, so we're not really in the room advocating for retail to get a bigger slice of the pie."
"When we got approved to serve as an underwriter, that changed," Tenev said. "And we said, we intend to be disruptive in the space because fundamentally, you look at the IPO process, and I think there's a lot that can be improved. Even from the issuer standpoint, you don't have a ton of visibility as to the demand, the price elasticity at different IPO prices. And I think through our work and IPO access, I think we've had a very, very unique view and a data-driven approach to answering some of these questions."
Tenev stopped short of promising an underwriting position on an upcoming hot IPO like Anthropic (ANTH.PVT).
"Obviously, I can't make any promises," Tenev said. "You should know that we're working hard across the board, making sure people are aware of our offerings and the advantages that we bring."

item.title: Musk's Boring Company snags $3 billion in latest fundraise
item.author: Pras Subramanian
item.description:
Musk's Boring Company snags $3 billion in latest fundraise
2026-09-11
Por Pras Subramanian
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/musks-boring-company-snags-3-billion-in-latest-fundraise-150209170.html
Add another notch to Elon Musk's fundraising exploits.
The Boring Company, Musk's tunnel-digging startup, announced it raised $3 billion in a Series D funding round, valuing the company at $23 billion. The latest round is led by the UAE and its various investment entities, with funds earmarked to expand an existing partnership to "deploy mass quantities of underground infrastructure across the United Arab Emirates (UAE), including 150+ kilometers of tunnel," the company said. This is separate from the Dubai Loop project that will start later this year.
In addition to the UAE, the other key investors in the round are a who's who of venture capital and private equity players, including Human Capital, Vy Capital, Valor Equity Partners, Sequoia Capital, A16Z, Temasek, Shamal Holding, and Baron Capital.
Boring notes that its new "Prufrock" tunnel-boring platform is the future of boring large volumes of earth to create tunnels for traffic and infrastructure. The company said in August this year that it successfully implemented a fully autonomous partial tunnel build, which is likely where the industry is headed with zero-people-in-pit (ZPIT).
To date, the only operating tunnel system created by Boring is the "Vegas Loop" in Las Vegas, which added new stations at Westgate, Encore, Fontainebleau, and Sahara Las Vegas, with an airport connector opening soon. Boring says 4 million passengers have used the service.
Boring says the next project, in addition to work in the UAE, will be the "Music City Loop" in Nashville that was announced last year. The Music City Loop will connect Nashville with Music City Center, Lower Broadway, and Nashville International Airport. Work began in February of this year.
Critics of Boring Company question whether the tunnels actually solve traffic issues, as they can only move so many people given their size and the number of vehicles that can pass through them, in addition to concerns about the complexity, environmental costs, and regulatory hurdles in construction.
Nevertheless, the latest fundraising round comes on the heels of Musk's massive SpaceX IPO, which raised $75 billion in the largest public offering ever. Prior to its IPO, SpaceX raised around $12 billion in private money per KeepTrack, a space-economy blog.
